highlights.content: TelcoNews Australia - Telecommunications news for ICT decision-makers [![TelcoNews Australia logo](/brands/tn-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.com.au) ![NVIDIA expands Australian AI infrastructure with partners](https://telconews.com.au/uploads/story/2026/09/14/neutral-australian-data-center-server-rows-network-lines-startup-laptop-university-office-modern-digital-illustration-story-318936.webp) [Cloud Security](https://telconews.com.au/tag/cloud-security) [Edge Computing](https://telconews.com.au/tag/edge-computing) [DC](https://telconews.com.au/tag/data-centers) # NVIDIA expands Australian AI infrastructure with partners Mon, 14th Sep 2026 (Today) [![Sean Mitchell](https://telconews.com.au/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyOSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a929a91c2a04d9af95ed98b14ed4d405bc70c1a7/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/IMG_3092.webp) SEAN MITCHELL Publisher](/author/sean-mitchell) NVIDIA has expanded its Australian AI infrastructure partnerships with Firmus, Sharon AI, IREN, Megaport, ResetData, CDC, NEXTDC and AirTrunk. The programme is intended to support up to a 2-gigawatt buildout by 2027. The expansion focuses on adding land, power and data centre shell capacity at sites designed to host multiple generations of NVIDIA DSX systems. Participating providers will operate the facilities, while NVIDIA will supply the DSX platform, computing systems, networking, software and ecosystem support. Demand for AI computing has risen as companies, researchers and public sector bodies seek more local access to large-scale infrastructure for training and deploying models. The broader buildout is intended to serve Australian startups, universities, researchers, developers, enterprises and AI-focused companies. NVIDIA also tied the expansion to broader use of its Nemotron open models in Australia, saying greater local access to computing resources and models would help organisations develop regional applications and agents for domestic industries. **Partner buildout** Several participating groups also outlined separate projects under the wider programme. Firmus is extending its Project Southgate initiative, which is intended to support demand from hyperscale operators and AI-focused customers in Australia and the Asia-Pacific region. “Project Southgate represents a tangible commitment to building Australia's AI future,” said Oliver Curtis, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Firmus. “Together with NVIDIA, we are developing AI factories that will give Australian businesses, researchers and innovators access to world-class computing capacity at home, while positioning Australia to meet growing AI demand across Asia-Pacific,” Curtis said. Sharon AI is deploying up to 68,000 NVIDIA GPUs linked with NVIDIA Quantum InfiniBand and NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. The infrastructure is intended to support startups, enterprises and research organisations. “Australia has the energy, connectivity and ambition to lead in AI. That potential only becomes real capability when organizations can access world-class compute without compromising on security or sovereignty,” said James Manning, Co-Founder and CEO of Sharon AI. “By building on NVIDIA's DSX platform, Sharon AI is equipped to bring gigawatt-scale AI factories to Australian enterprises, researchers, government and AI natives. With the trust and reliability needed to build, train and deploy AI at scale, Australia can turn its natural advantages into a genuine national AI capability,” Manning said. highlights.titleZh: Are we losing control of AI? What’s driving new fears
highlights.content: [![Straitstimes.com header logo](/assets/ST-logo-default-aoeSLh4S.png)](https://www.straitstimes.com) # Are we losing control of AI? What’s driving new fears [Sign up now:](/newsletter-signup?ref=inline-article) Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Top AI executives like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (left) and OpenAI chief Sam Altman (right) say they want to slow the breakneck pace of artificial intelligence development. PHOTOS: AFP Published Sep 15, 2026, 07:55 AM Updated Sep 15, 2026, 07:55 AM For years, as artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from the stuff of science fiction movies to an app ordinary people have installed on their phones, tech leaders and some AI insiders have talked about the potential for it to escape human control and wreak havoc on society. Those fears have become impossible to ignore in recent days, driven by advances in the technology, a series of cybersecurity breaches involving AI agents, and new warnings from rank-and-file AI staff. Leading AI companies in the US have responded by suggesting they voluntarily slow their work to buy time to create safeguards. Some experts and officials say that is not good enough and are urging government restrictions. ## What sparked the current AI panic? The current AI panic was sparked by two developments – a startling cyberattack carried out by OpenAI models and a warning from a former Anthropic PBC and OpenAI employee about [the existential threat posed by advanced models](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/openai-ipo-will-not-happen-in-2026-amid-ai-safety-fears-chief-sam-altman-says?ref=inline-article). OpenAI said [a swarm of advanced AI agents inadvertently hacked Hugging Face,](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/openai-agents-hacked-hugging-face-in-700-strong-swarm-tried-to-cover-tracks-investigations?ref=inline-article) which hosts AI models and datasets, in an “unprecedented” incident in July. While operating in a “sandbox” testing environment – one designed to be isolated from the internet – OpenAI’s models exploited a vulnerability in the software of an unidentified third-party vendor to gain access to the internet and [ultimately breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure.](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/openai-agents-attacked-rubygems-before-hugging-face-incident-researchers-say?ref=inline-article) OpenAI said the models targeted Hugging Face’s database to gain access to secret information they could use for the evaluation. The incident caused widespread alarm about the ability of top AI firms to prevent and stop advanced AI models from operating outside their intended instructions. Hugging Face said the intrusion was “driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system”. The OpenAI news prompted other companies to review their own security measures for testing advanced AI. Anthropic and Meta reported discovering previously unknown breaches. In late July, more than 1,000 staff across all the major AI companies signed a petition calling for a mechanism to slow the pace of AI development. After quitting his job at Anthropic, rank-and-file AI researcher Jacob Coxon, in a Sept 8 social media post, accused both the company and his former employer, OpenAI, of [“gambling with our lives”](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/theyre-playing-with-our-lives-ai-researcher-quits-anthropic?ref=inline-article) by “racing toward super-intelligent AI”. Coxon said the people building AI believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade,” a point later echoed online by Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger. Hubinger said he believes there is a greater than 10 per cent chance that AI eliminates all humans in the next decade. Coxon’s posts have been viewed more than 170 million times on X as of Sept 14 and elicited [a flood of calls from policymakers](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/us-lawmakers-call-for-new-ai-rules-after-anthropic-researchers-safety-warnings?ref=inline-article) such as Senator Bernie Sa...

highlights.content: BEIJING, September 14 - Warnings from researchers at ​leading U.S. artificial intelligence developer Anthropic that increasingly powerful models could escape human control and even lead to the extinction of the human race have drawn ‌attention in China, where policymakers have been preparing for some of the same risks. The U.S. and China are the two major driving forces of frontier AI development and the technology's global adoption. Both superpowers have been increasingly at loggerheads over each other's AI policies and industry practices, with these issues slated to feature prominently in bilateral talks later this month. Sign up here. Despite the race to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, regulatory frameworks and public ​statements from Beijing underscore how Chinese authorities regard the possibility of advanced AI escaping effective human oversight as serious enough to plan for. ## CHINA SEES RISKS IN LEADING ​CLOSED-SOURCE U.S. MODELS China's state security minister Chen Yixin wrote in a government outlet on Sunday that advanced U.S. models such as Anthropic's Mythos ⁠and OpenAI's GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to China's critical information infrastructure, and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security. Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to Reuters requests ​for comment. Chinese AI developers have promoted open-weight models partly on the grounds that cybersecurity teams can inspect, modify and deploy them for defensive work. Model repository platform Hugging Face said it used ​GLM-5.2, an open-weight model developed by China's Z.AI (2513.HK), to analyse a July intrusion by escaped OpenAI agents after more tightly restricted U.S. models proved less useful for the forensic work. But experts also highlight the risks posed by open-weight models, which can be modified and redistributed with little oversight. Moonshot's Kimi K3 last month bypassed a UK AI Security Institute testing sandbox, highlighting the risk that Chinese AI models could, like their ​U.S. counterparts, evade controls designed to restrict their access and actions. ## REGULATORS HAVE FLAGGED AI 'LOSS OF CONTROL' RISK China first included an explicit future loss-of-control scenario in an AI safety framework released ​in September 2024 under the guidance of the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC). The document said it could not be ruled out that future AI might autonomously obtain external resources, replicate itself, develop self-awareness and seek ‌external power, ⁠creating a risk of competing with humans for control. The CAC released an expanded version in September 2025. The newer framework sharpened the scenario, saying AI could undergo a sudden and unexpectedly large "leap" in intelligence before acquiring resources, replicating itself and seeking power. It also added a governance principle of "trusted application, preventing loss of control". A later expert interpretation published on the cyberspace regulator's website said the new principle was intended to guard against loss-of-control risks threatening human survival and development and referred to a possible "AI breaking loose" scenario. ## CHINESE LEADER XI PUTS HUMAN CONTROL AT ​CENTRE The concern has since appeared in China's highest-level ​political messaging. At the World Artificial Intelligence ⁠Conference in Shanghai in July, Chinese President Xi Jinping said authorities should pay close attention to both intrinsic and derivative risks arising from AI. He said AI should "always remain under human control". China's senior Foreign Ministry official responsible for AI affairs, Sun Xiaobo, said at a United Nations meeting ​last month that China was accelerating research into broader AI legislation. China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, Sun Lei, urged governments ​this month to approach ⁠military AI cautiously to avoid strategic miscalculation and an arms race. ## BEIJING WARNS OF NEW RISKS POSED BY AI AGENTS China has, mean...

AI Agents.content: [![Straitstimes.com header logo](/assets/ST-logo-default-aoeSLh4S.png)](https://www.straitstimes.com) # Are we losing control of AI? What’s driving new fears [Sign up now:](/newsletter-signup?ref=inline-article) Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Top AI executives like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (left) and OpenAI chief Sam Altman (right) say they want to slow the breakneck pace of artificial intelligence development. PHOTOS: AFP Published Sep 15, 2026, 07:55 AM Updated Sep 15, 2026, 07:55 AM For years, as artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from the stuff of science fiction movies to an app ordinary people have installed on their phones, tech leaders and some AI insiders have talked about the potential for it to escape human control and wreak havoc on society. Those fears have become impossible to ignore in recent days, driven by advances in the technology, a series of cybersecurity breaches involving AI agents, and new warnings from rank-and-file AI staff. Leading AI companies in the US have responded by suggesting they voluntarily slow their work to buy time to create safeguards. Some experts and officials say that is not good enough and are urging government restrictions. ## What sparked the current AI panic? The current AI panic was sparked by two developments – a startling cyberattack carried out by OpenAI models and a warning from a former Anthropic PBC and OpenAI employee about [the existential threat posed by advanced models](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/openai-ipo-will-not-happen-in-2026-amid-ai-safety-fears-chief-sam-altman-says?ref=inline-article). OpenAI said [a swarm of advanced AI agents inadvertently hacked Hugging Face,](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/openai-agents-hacked-hugging-face-in-700-strong-swarm-tried-to-cover-tracks-investigations?ref=inline-article) which hosts AI models and datasets, in an “unprecedented” incident in July. While operating in a “sandbox” testing environment – one designed to be isolated from the internet – OpenAI’s models exploited a vulnerability in the software of an unidentified third-party vendor to gain access to the internet and [ultimately breached Hugging Face’s infrastructure.](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/openai-agents-attacked-rubygems-before-hugging-face-incident-researchers-say?ref=inline-article) OpenAI said the models targeted Hugging Face’s database to gain access to secret information they could use for the evaluation. The incident caused widespread alarm about the ability of top AI firms to prevent and stop advanced AI models from operating outside their intended instructions. Hugging Face said the intrusion was “driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system”. The OpenAI news prompted other companies to review their own security measures for testing advanced AI. Anthropic and Meta reported discovering previously unknown breaches. In late July, more than 1,000 staff across all the major AI companies signed a petition calling for a mechanism to slow the pace of AI development. After quitting his job at Anthropic, rank-and-file AI researcher Jacob Coxon, in a Sept 8 social media post, accused both the company and his former employer, OpenAI, of [“gambling with our lives”](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/theyre-playing-with-our-lives-ai-researcher-quits-anthropic?ref=inline-article) by “racing toward super-intelligent AI”. Coxon said the people building AI believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade,” a point later echoed online by Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger. Hubinger said he believes there is a greater than 10 per cent chance that AI eliminates all humans in the next decade. Coxon’s posts have been viewed more than 170 million times on X as of Sept 14 and elicited [a flood of calls from policymakers](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/united-states/us-lawmakers-call-for-new-ai-rules-after-anthropic-researchers-safety-warnings?ref=inline-article) such as Senator Bernie Sa...

AI Agents.title: How China is preparing for the risk of AI escaping human control
AI Agents.titleZh: How China is preparing for the risk of AI escaping human control
AI Agents.content: BEIJING, September 14 - Warnings from researchers at ​leading U.S. artificial intelligence developer Anthropic that increasingly powerful models could escape human control and even lead to the extinction of the human race have drawn ‌attention in China, where policymakers have been preparing for some of the same risks. The U.S. and China are the two major driving forces of frontier AI development and the technology's global adoption. Both superpowers have been increasingly at loggerheads over each other's AI policies and industry practices, with these issues slated to feature prominently in bilateral talks later this month. Sign up here. Despite the race to develop increasingly powerful AI systems, regulatory frameworks and public ​statements from Beijing underscore how Chinese authorities regard the possibility of advanced AI escaping effective human oversight as serious enough to plan for. ## CHINA SEES RISKS IN LEADING ​CLOSED-SOURCE U.S. MODELS China's state security minister Chen Yixin wrote in a government outlet on Sunday that advanced U.S. models such as Anthropic's Mythos ⁠and OpenAI's GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to China's critical information infrastructure, and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security. Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to Reuters requests ​for comment. Chinese AI developers have promoted open-weight models partly on the grounds that cybersecurity teams can inspect, modify and deploy them for defensive work. Model repository platform Hugging Face said it used ​GLM-5.2, an open-weight model developed by China's Z.AI (2513.HK), to analyse a July intrusion by escaped OpenAI agents after more tightly restricted U.S. models proved less useful for the forensic work. But experts also highlight the risks posed by open-weight models, which can be modified and redistributed with little oversight. Moonshot's Kimi K3 last month bypassed a UK AI Security Institute testing sandbox, highlighting the risk that Chinese AI models could, like their ​U.S. counterparts, evade controls designed to restrict their access and actions. ## REGULATORS HAVE FLAGGED AI 'LOSS OF CONTROL' RISK China first included an explicit future loss-of-control scenario in an AI safety framework released ​in September 2024 under the guidance of the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC). The document said it could not be ruled out that future AI might autonomously obtain external resources, replicate itself, develop self-awareness and seek ‌external power, ⁠creating a risk of competing with humans for control. The CAC released an expanded version in September 2025. The newer framework sharpened the scenario, saying AI could undergo a sudden and unexpectedly large "leap" in intelligence before acquiring resources, replicating itself and seeking power. It also added a governance principle of "trusted application, preventing loss of control". A later expert interpretation published on the cyberspace regulator's website said the new principle was intended to guard against loss-of-control risks threatening human survival and development and referred to a possible "AI breaking loose" scenario. ## CHINESE LEADER XI PUTS HUMAN CONTROL AT ​CENTRE The concern has since appeared in China's highest-level ​political messaging. At the World Artificial Intelligence ⁠Conference in Shanghai in July, Chinese President Xi Jinping said authorities should pay close attention to both intrinsic and derivative risks arising from AI. He said AI should "always remain under human control". China's senior Foreign Ministry official responsible for AI affairs, Sun Xiaobo, said at a United Nations meeting ​last month that China was accelerating research into broader AI legislation. The CEO of Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind Claude, said he thought the industry needed to reduce the speed of its work, cautioning Saturday that a swarm of AI agents might be able to take over the internet in six months to a year unless companies devoted more time to putting safeguards in place. [**READ MORE:** Anthropic CEO says AI industry needs to give safety measures time to catch up](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/anthropic-ceo-says-ai-industry-needs-to-give-safety-measures-time-to-catch-up) Dario Amodei outlined a plan for companies like his and governments around the world to ensure that increasingly capable AI models remain aligned with the commands and values of responsible people days after two former Anthropic safety researchers publicly aired concerns that the existential threats AI might pose to humanity were receiving too little attention. ## Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. LLMs.content: ![Forbes](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/e2a3ae2de696de290ce5ff45e647f96c40b4b3292b15aace10b1b05543020c37/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_h100%3Bquality_100%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fd29szjachogqwa.cloudfront.net%2Fimages%2Fuser-uploaded%2Fforbes-light.png) ![Forbes](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/7a1b49c388baebb0726b1fa37e92b672159504e0b170a6c6cd277ab77752f172/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_h100%3Bquality_100%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fd29szjachogqwa.cloudfront.net%2Fimages%2Fuser-uploaded%2Fforbes-dark.png) # Cognichip Creates Physics-Informed AI Models To Speed Chip Design ![Cognichip says its AI is the first to use a physics-informed foundation model.](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/2f744d1e8393333a5f990ea901886034b33a01ed53e71c9a30e8326cbc4e4059/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w959_h494%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fforbes_contributor_845%2Fa5a7b97594acb9f0b8c51e41006f732b.png) Cognichip says its AI is the first to use a physics-informed foundation model. As I described in [a recent article](https://www.forbes.com/sites/karlfreund/2026/08/03/could-eda-ai-startups-be-the-new-claude-of-chip-design/), several chip design startups are working to revolutionize chip design with AI, just as Anthropic's Claude Code has revolutionized software development. Could we be approaching the day when AI can design a finished chip just from the specifications? With Cognichip's AI Chip Intelligence (ACI) announcement, we just took a huge step in that direction. Instead of using agentic AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), Cognichip took a unique approach and developed physics-based AI models to automate each step in chip design. Details will be presented at this week's AI Infra Summit being held in Santa Clara. How good is this new approach? Manoher Bommena, a Vice President of Engineering at semiconductor firm Renesas, said "Cognichip's ACI represents one of the most comprehensive approaches to bringing AI into the contemporary design environment – it simply 'speaks chip'". Early results point to a roughly 100 times speedup of chip design, with lower power, higher performance, and lower chip cost. The company has raised $93 million in total funding from Mayfield Fund, Lux Capital, FPV Ventures, Seligman Ventures, SBI Investment, and Candou Ventures. Let's dive in. ## The Cognichip ACI Full-Stack Design System Most chip design AI tools today are based either on reinforcement learning, such as physical layout tools, or a wrapper around a Large Language Model (LLM), which are trained on a massive amount of text and a relatively small sample of chip design data. One reason we haven't seen a model trained on chip design is the lack of available data for training such a model. Chip design details are notoriously well-kept secrets, so there simply isn't enough public data to train a neural network adequately. Cognichip made a strategic bet and built their foundation models on the experiences of its own design team and synthetic data, taking the data sparsity challenge in semiconductors head-on. ![Instead of wrapping AI around EDA tools, Cognichip built its platform from the ground up on AI.](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/dc81a0c6412821703b8308503048a9273d54b9060c99078de9f7938a3d93c392/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w959_h494%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fforbes_contributor_845%2Fdadeeae07f51c4bbe39397c4605ea38e.png) Instead of wrapping AI around EDA tools, Cognichip built its platform from the ground up on AI. Convinced the industry needed a better solution than wrapping agentic AI around LLMs, the company solved the data problem by staffing a chip design project with experienced engineers. They then complemented that approach with a team of AI scientists to create synthetic data to train the AI models. "Every day, tens of thousands of videos of pelicans riding bicycles are posted to groups in the community, asking me if this pelican has lost its intelligence." Lambda, initiator of the open-source project CodexRadar, received a huge number of pelican videos every day after the release of GPT-6 Astra, so he simply launched a "Pelican Cup" competition in the community. Participants take the task of "drawing a pelican riding a bicycle" to generate works with the model, and then send the results to the community. "It went online late at night, and we received nearly a hundred submissions without any promotion." Lambda did not expect that everyone's enthusiasm for the "pelican test" was so high. Every time a new model is launched, some people will use a pelican riding a bicycle to test the model's capabilities. On the one hand, this task is simple and intuitive enough. Many complex capabilities of the model are difficult to judge quickly with a single sentence, but a pelican riding a bicycle makes it very easy to see the stability at a glance, such as whether the legs are aligned with the pedals, whether the wheels are moving accordingly, whether the movements have obvious flaws, and whether the generation is consistent before and after. On the other hand, this task is complex enough. It seems to be just a short prompt, but behind it involves action understanding, temporal consistency, spatial relationship, code organization and continuous execution capabilities. For a model that has entered the Agent stage, this kind of task is very suitable to act as a "physical feeling thermometer". After GPT-6 Astra went online, this pelican became even more popular. The reason is that this most advanced model has very unstable "intelligence", which will have a direct impact on work results. The pelican just makes this kind of hard-to-quantify physical feeling very intuitive. ## **01 How Does a Pelican Test Whether the Model Has "Lost Intelligence"** The Pelican Cup competition is divided into two tracks. The Classic track uses a unified prompt: "Create an HTML file containing a 2D animation of a pelican riding a bicycle drawn with SVG". As long as the model is in normal state, the pelican generated by GPT-6 Astra usually maintains relatively consistent quality and picture structure. Figure: The pelican image uploaded by users to social networks shows that if the intelligence of GPT-6 Astra remains stable under various inference intensities, the generated pelican images are basically consistent If a large number of users suddenly find one day that under the same prompt, the pelican starts to frequently miss the pedal, the wheel relationship is disordered, and the structure is obviously deviated, discussions about "intelligence loss" will quickly emerge. This method certainly cannot be called a strict scientific benchmark. A publicly available question repeated at high frequency also has the possibility of being gradually familiarized by the model. But it is very suitable for observing short-term changes in physical feeling. Users do not need to understand complex indicators, and can spot differences just by looking at a few pelicans. Figure: Screenshot of the works of the "Pelican Cup", marking the "intelligence-lost" works, you can see that the pelican is "obviously wrong" The Open track does not set a unified prompt, and participants can give full play to their creativity freely. It is more like testing how far Astra can go with an open task. One of the works was finally made into a 30-minute "one-shot" cycling story. LLMs.titleZh: Hyundai Sets 2029 Self-Driving Deadline: Language-Reasoning AI ...
LLMs.content: One day after Hyundai Motor Group held its "HMG Autonomous Driving Media Day" at 42dot headquarters in Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, the group's autonomous driving roadmap now has the most specific public timeline the group has ever committed to: Level 2+ production vehicles built on NVIDIA hardware arriving in the first half of 2028, followed by Level 2++ NVIDIA-based vehicles in the second half of 2028, and fully proprietary Level 2++ cars powered by its in-house Atria AI arriving in the second half of 2029. The September 13 announcement also declared the group's AI-powered Data Flywheel fully operational — a four-stage continuous learning pipeline that draws training data from roughly 7 million vehicles sold annually across the Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis brands. The announcement was made at 42dot headquarters in Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, and represents a public accountability moment: specific dates, named architectures, and footage of the AI navigating Seoul's streets. What separates this roadmap from a standard automaker press event is the technical bet at its center. Hyundai is not simply building a larger version of what Tesla or Waymo already use. Its proprietary Atria AI system relies on a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model — an architecture that inserts a language-reasoning step between what the car's cameras see and what its steering and throttle do. The VLA research literature treats that reasoning step as the specific lever for handling the long-tail edge cases that stump systems trained purely to mimic human driving patterns. Whether Hyundai can make that bet pay off at production scale — and on a timeline measured in years rather than decades — is the question the group's new roadmap asks readers to judge. The strategic foundation for Atria AI is what Hyundai calls the Data Flywheel — a four-stage continuous learning pipeline that its announcement describes as now fully operational. The mechanism works as follows: production vehicles collect real-world driving data, software identifies the specific scenarios where the current AI model underperformed (a process called hard example mining), those failure cases feed back into a continuous retraining pipeline, and an updated model is redeployed to the fleet over the air. The strategic logic borrows from a playbook that Tesla pioneered and Waymo independently developed. By early 2026, Tesla's equivalent system had reportedly ingested more than 9 billion miles of supervised driving data, while Waymo uses what it calls an "outer learning loop" that automatically flags suboptimal driving behaviors from its commercial robotaxi fleet and routes them into simulation for retraining. Hyundai's advantage, if the flywheel executes as described, is distribution: with roughly 7 million vehicles sold annually across the Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis brands, the group has a passive data-collection network that no dedicated AV startup can match. The operative challenge — which the flywheel framework does not fully resolve by itself — is data quality rather than volume. Hard example mining addresses this by filtering for scenarios the current model fails on. Hyundai pairs this with a Special Event Recorder (SER) system that automatically records and stores significant events and related data during autonomous driving operations, feeding those events back into AI model training and performance improvement. What Current Research Really Shows ![Suyash Raizada](/blog-media/authors/QHoc5VfTtKij/avatar.jpg) ![Can AI Train AI Models Without Humans? What Current Research Really Shows](/_next/image/?url=%2Fblog-media%2Fposts%2F8dbe81ef-f76%2Fcan-ai-train-ai-models-without-humans-what-current-research-really-shows.jpg&w=1920&q=75) **Can AI train AI models without humans?** Yes, in narrow and increasingly impressive ways. AI systems can now generate tasks, label data, score answers, create synthetic datasets, and run self-play loops that improve model behavior with little day-to-day human input. But fully human-free training of the next generation of frontier AI models is not ready for safe, general deployment. Humans still set the goals, write the rules, choose architectures, control compute, and decide what is acceptable in the real world. Anyone trying to build a working understanding of this space often starts with a structured credential like the [**Certified Artificial Intelligence (AI) Expert**](https://www.blockchain-council.org/certifications/certified-artificial-intelligence-ai-expert/), which lays out where automation genuinely helps and where human judgment is still required. That distinction matters. A model can teach itself to solve coding puzzles. It cannot, by itself, decide what a hospital chatbot should refuse, what a legal assistant should cite, or when a self-improving agent should be stopped. ![Certified Artificial Intelligence Expert Ad Strip](/blog-ads/email-strip/certified-agentic-ai-expert.png) ## What Does "AI Training AI" Actually Mean? When researchers talk about AI training AI, they usually mean models are taking over parts of the training pipeline that humans used to do by hand. Those parts include: Generating prompts, tasks, and examples Creating synthetic data for training Producing labels for unlabeled data Scoring model answers as a reward signal Selecting harder examples as the model improves Critiquing unsafe or low-quality outputs This is not science fiction. It already happens in modern machine learning teams. A common workflow uses a stronger model to label thousands or millions of examples, then trains a smaller model on that output. Another lets a reasoning model generate coding or math problems, solve them, validate the answers with a tool such as Python, and train on the successful attempts. Practitioners looking to move from reading about these pipelines to actually building them often pursue the [**Certified Artificial Intelligence (AI) Developer**](https://www.blockchain-council.org/certifications/certified-artificial-intelligence-ai-developer/) track, which focuses on hands-on implementation rather than theory alone. There is still a hidden human layer underneath. People decide the loss function, the benchmark, the safety policy, the deployment environment, and the point at which a model is good enough to ship. ## The Main Ways AI Trains Other AI Models ### Self-Supervised Learning and Pseudo-Labeling Self-supervised learning is the foundation of most large language models. The model learns from raw text by predicting missing or next tokens, without a person labeling each sentence. Pseudo-labeling takes this further. A trained model generates labels for unlabeled data, filters the most confident ones, and uses them to train a new model. MIT researchers have explored fast self-training, where a pre-trained model labels raw data, keeps high-confidence predictions, and retrains iteratively. This cuts the need for manual annotation, especially in domains where labels are costly. A practical warning: confidence filtering is not magic. LLMs.title: Does AI Have Low EQ? USC Study Identifies Where Models’ Emotional Reasoning Breaks Down
LLMs.titleZh: Does AI Have Low EQ? USC Study Identifies Where Models’ Emotional Reasoning Breaks Down
LLMs.content: [![Image](https://viterbischool.usc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/USC-Shield-BlackBG.png)](https://usc.edu/) [![Formal](https://viterbischool.usc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Formal-Viterbi-Logo-New.png)](/) --- [School of Engineering](/) # Does AI Have Low EQ? USC Study Identifies Where Models’ Emotional Reasoning Breaks Down Venice Tang | September 14, 2026  USC Viterbi and USC Stevens engineers reveal how AI models misinterpret emotional cues from audio and video, and introduce a framework to help them reason with real evidence ![Illustration of a robot staring at a red heart. (Credit: Midjourney)](https://viterbischool.usc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/1200-x-600-article-feature-photos-23.png) AI emotional reasoning through audios and videos (Credit: Midjourney) Have you ever interacted with an AI-powered customer support agent only to find it strangely nonempathetic, cold, disconnected and unable to understand how you’re feeling? Unlike humans, AI does not actually experience emotions. Instead, it can appear to understand emotions by using logic to infer them from audio and visual cues — a capability known as emotion reasoning. This ability is often found in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), advanced AI systems that can understand and analyze multiple types of data, like images, audio, video and text, simultaneously. However, today’s AI technologies still face significant limitations in emotion reasoning, often hallucinating or completely mislabeling how people feel. These errors can compromise the reliability of AI agents in social interactions and other complex emotion reasoning scenarios. USC researcher [Mohammad Soleymani](https://viterbi.usc.edu/directory/faculty/Soleymani/Mohammad) led a study investigating why AI models fail to associate audiovisual cues with the correct emotions and how to “debug AI’s logic” by proposing a new optimization framework that helps ensure emotional judgments are logically grounded in actual evidence. Findings of ILTA’s Tech Survey May Surprise You](https://www.lawnext.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ILTA-2026-Survey-Cover.png) By [Bob Ambrogi](https://www.lawnext.com/author/ambrogi) on Tweet ![twitter]() Share ![linkedin]() Share ![facebook]() At the recent conference of the International Legal Technology Association, the big legal AI vendors CoCounsel, Harvey and Legora had outsized presences, with ginormous booths in the exhibit hall, major-name performers at their parties, and advertising so ubiquitous it even popped up in people’s Uber apps. (See: [Have We Reached ‘Peak Legal Tech?’ Sure Felt That Way At ILTACON this Week](https://www.lawnext.com/2026/08/have-we-reached-peak-legal-tech-sure-felt-that-way-at-iltacon-this-week.html).) So which of those is the preferred choice of law firms? Turns out, the answer is “None of the above,” at least according to the findings of the [just released 2026 technology survey](https://www.iltanet.org/resources/publications/surveys/ts26). The survey spanned over 500 law firms — all ILTA members — from small boutiques to global giants, representing a dozen countries and 140,000 lawyers. Of them, the vast majority, 94%, say they are using or exploring generative AI tools, up from 80% last year. But when ILTA asked the firms which tool they are using or exploring, the leader by a wide margin was Microsoft 365 Copilot, used by 76% of firms. Second place was effectively a three-way tie between two of the leading legal AI products, Thomson Reuters CoCounsel (44%) and Harvey (43%), and one non-legal general AI product, Anthropic’s Claude (44%). Legora came in much lower in the results, at 16%, behind products such as Lexis+AI (26%), ChatGPT Enterprise (22%), iManage (22%) and Litera One (17%). Breaking that down by firm size shows interesting patterns. Among firms of fewer than 50 lawyers, Copilot retains its top position (59%), followed again by Claude (42%) and CoCounsel (40%), but Harvey drops to 22% and Legora to 6%. At the other end of the size spectrum, among firms of 700 or more lawyers, the gap narrows between Copilot and Harvey, with Copilot seeing usage among 88% of firms and Harvey among 84%. But even among those large firms, Claude still gets 64% of usage, ahead of Legora (47%) and CoCounsel (43%). ### Deployment vs. Piloting It is one thing for a firm to say it is using one or more of these AI products, but it is another thing entirely to consider where these firms are in their AI deployment. Here again, the survey offers some revealing data. Only two AI products in the survey have been fully deployed by at least half of respondent firms’ lawyers: Microsoft Copilot, with 52% of firms reporting full deployment among lawyers, and Westlaw Advantage, with 50% of firms reporting full deployment. However, here is where the survey results get a bit confusing, as the Copilot that leads in deployment is not Microsoft 365 Copilot, which is a paid product, but, as the survey puts it, “Microsoft Copilot (formerly Bing Chat),” which would appear to be the free version included in Windows. But the survey also provides results for “Microsoft Copilot for Windows.” Microsoft’s own website [lists three versions with different names](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/copilot/microsoft-365-copilot-overview?tabs=microsoft-copilot-chat-basic%2Cmicrosoft-copilot-chat-basic-training) than those used in the survey: Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot (Basic) and Microsoft 365 Copilot (Premium). The products are designed to let non-technical users review an AI agent's work before relying on the output of a data workflow or chart. AI Product.content: As AI rages on, new startups are creating tools for people to create music using generative AI prompts in the style of any artist they want. A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya, a startup that sounds more like an indie band name, is focused on releasing a series of small apps that let you play around with sounds and vocals. The company has raised a $5.5m pre-seed round from Mantis VC, SV Angel, Boxgroup, Quiet Capital, Remarkable Ventures, Common Metal, Gold House, Liquid 2 Ventures, Breakers VC, Collaborative Fund, Systemic Ventures, and former Spotify chief content and advertising business officer, Dawn Ostroff, who joined the company as an advisor. The startup is built by Máuhan M Zonoozy, who was the former head of innovation at Spotify. Prior to that, he founded a video clipping and remixing startup called Bubbl, which was acquired by Cricket Media. Zonoozy, who left Spotify in 2024, said that he always wanted to go back to building something of his own. He thought that while streaming solved the access problem, most of the interaction with music was still around consumption. “I think when I looked at emergent behaviors and younger audiences, like everyone’s growing up playing with culture through games, through filters, through creation tools. And I just felt like there was an opportunity to empower people to do something similar with music,” he told TechCrunch. The startup releases these experiments like “singles” that are part of an album. The common theme between all of these apps or websites is interacting with different elements to create music or modify sound. For instance, Speed Surfer is a Chrome extension that changes the speed and filter of sound playing in your browser window. Usersound is a website where you can create an “audio” username with each letter representing a note. Stacks is a stem player where you can create mixes by turning bars on or off in a 3×3 grid. Drops is about placing plaques in a pattern to deflect marbles falling down, which creates musical notes. Sampler is a website that turns YouTube videos into music samplers based on beats of different parts of the songs. The company’s more ambitious product is an iOS app called bop. This lets you place musical instruments and effects in a grid to create different mixes of a base song. You can also adjust tempo and add one-time effects. Once you create these mixes, you can easily export them to TikTok or Instagram. A Vinyl Bar in Shibuya is also working on a multiplayer version, which would let users remix songs with others. The company recently added a prompt-based feature to create a sound. Zonoozy said that it is making an informed choice not to infuse AI into every part of these apps. He is open to using AI to build these products and to make infrastructure solid, though. “AI is obviously extraordinarily powerful, but I think we just don’t necessarily believe that the future of music is simply generation, like song generation via AI. And I think if AI starts to make that content more abundant, it actually makes taste and human perspective and interaction and participation even more important and even more valuable. And we’re just trying to make sure it doesn’t make it even rarer,” he said. This year, the company aims to release a “musical sandbox mixer” product that would let users play around with different elements of music-making, including being able to create instruments. The story title was changed because, at the time of testing last month, there were no prompt-based features in the startup’s apps. The company added prompt-based features more recently to its apps. By **[Abid Ali Awan](https://www.kdnuggets.com/author/abidali-awan)**, KDnuggets Assistant Editor on September 14, 2026 in [Language Models](https://www.kdnuggets.com/tag/language-models) --- DeepSeek has released **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash**, and while the benchmark numbers are impressive, they are probably not the most interesting part of this release. The architecture is. DeepSeek is tackling several problems that are becoming increasingly important as AI moves toward long-running agents: **expensive prefill, huge KV caches, long contexts, memory bandwidth, and the cost of maintaining agent state across interactions**. Rather than simply making the model larger, DeepSeek has redesigned several parts of the architecture and inference stack to make long-context AI much cheaper to run. MCP’s usage has grown at an astonishing rate. Across MCP’s Tier 1 SDKs, monthly downloads are approaching half a billion, with both the TypeScript and Python SDKs surpassing 1 billion downloads total. Usage in production is climbing just as fast. MCP tool calls from ChatGPT users reached 98 times their January level by August, and Resend passed one million MCP calls in a single month. That scale is exactly why a common way to validate MCP expertise is needed. The MCPA provides engineers, platform teams, and AI governance professionals a way to demonstrate their understanding of how the protocol works, how its components interact, and how to apply it responsibly. ![](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/05/Agentic-AI-Foundation-AAIF-300x157.jpg) “We built MCP so developers could rely on one open protocol instead of writing custom integrations for every system. Since then, it has grown exponentially. Giving developers the option to earn a certification in MCP will formalize a shared understanding of how the protocol works, while ensuring this expanding ecosystem continues to operate smoothly,” said David Soria Parra, co-creator and lead maintainer of MCP. The MCPA is a 120-minute, online, proctored, multiple-choice exam covering five domains: MCP Fundamentals (16%), Architecture & Components (14%), Interactions & Execution (26%), Security & Governance (24%), and Use Cases & Ecosystem (20%). Candidates are tested on MCP hosts, clients, servers, and tools; message flow and protocol primitives; trust boundaries, permissions, and risk controls; and how MCP is applied across real-world agentic deployments. Open Source AI.content: # OpenHunterAI releases an AI red-team engine after killing the startup **The local-first alpha tests web, API and LLM apps, while its noncommercial license preserves a route back to paid software.** By [Ryan Merket](/author/ryan-merket) · Published Primary source: [X - Nicolas Krassas](https://x.com/Dinosn/status/2099505079048945883) ## Why it matters OpenHunterAI shows one path for abandoned AI startups: release the core product for distribution, retain commercial rights and let adoption test whether a business remains. [Nicolas Krassas (@Dinosn)](https://x.com/Dinosn) said [in a post on X](https://x.com/Dinosn/status/2099505079048945883) on September 14th that his group had abandoned plans for an AI security startup and released its red-team engine as [OpenHunterAI](https://github.com/LumosLab-Innovation/OpenHunterAI). "We killed the startup idea and released the red-team engine instead," Krassas wrote. The decision puts the code in developers' hands while preserving the option to charge for commercial use, a narrower bet than building and selling another hosted security platform from scratch. Krassas brings an operator's background to that decision. His [public profile](https://ch.linkedin.com/in/nicolas-krassas) lists threat and vulnerability management work at Henkel, penetration testing and security leadership roles, along with earlier work securing the official Athens 2004 Olympics website. He also studied neural networks at the University of Leeds, giving the project a technical lineage that predates the current rush to attach language models to application-security scanners. OpenHunterAI runs on a user's machine through Docker Compose and is designed to assess verified public websites, APIs and LLM applications. Users define a target, verify its domain, authorize a scope and approve a scan plan before workers begin testing. The interface collects scan activity, evidence, findings, remediation guidance and manual retests in one local workspace. The product combines browser inspection, reconnaissance, OWASP ZAP and an adapter for the Nuclei vulnerability scanner. AI models assist with triage, attack hypotheses and remediation guidance. Users supply their own model-provider credentials, and the documentation cautions that local hosting does not make the system fully offline: requests can still reach external model providers and the target under assessment. OpenHunterAI also includes a skill that lets coding agents prepare assessments from inside an application repository. The published installation command names Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Grok Build as supported clients. The skill starts with a read-only helper and requires human approval before a scan begins. ### The release is an alpha, with blockers documented in the repo The public repository is unusually direct about what remains unfinished. Its [release-readiness review](https://github.com/LumosLab-Innovation/OpenHunterAI/blob/main/docs/PUBLIC_RELEASE_READINESS.md) labels OpenHunterAI an alpha and says the review covers source code rather than evidence from a fresh production deployment or a complete target scan. One blocker concerns Nuclei. OpenHunterAI packages an adapter, but the reviewed template bundle and its configuration are incomplete. The review warns that process errors can appear as an empty successful result because one execution path parses output without fully handling the underlying process failure. OpenHunterAI's own documentation tells users to resolve that blocker before scanning. OpenHack and Strix, two other security runtimes referenced by the project, must also be installed separately. The readiness review calls for a complete authorized end-to-end scan, including callbacks, reports, exports and manual retesting, after the blockers are fixed. Open Source AI.title: All Eyes Are on What Trump and Xi Will Do Amid Warnings of AI Doom - Business Insider
Open Source AI.titleZh: All Eyes Are on What Trump and Xi Will Do Amid Warnings of AI Doom - Business Insider
Open Source AI.content: In the face of a grim debate about an AI-fueled apocalypse, both President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are locked in on keeping up the pace of AI progress, not slowing it down. Trump downplayed concerns about AI researchers' warnings that AI could threaten humanity's existence during his visit to Ireland to watch the Irish Open. "Whoever wins AI, wins," Trump said from his Doonbeg golf resort. "And we can put guard rails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up, and they're bringing up things that won't happen," he added. Meanwhile, Xi has not directly commented on the AI doom-and-gloom yet. Instead, he said during a BRICS Summit in New Delhi on Sunday that "Global South" countries — developing countries in Asia, Africa, and South America — should work faster to create a global AI governance framework. He also said China would pioneer a BRICS open-source AI community that would support LLM development, host AI seminars, and build an open AI ecosystem. "We should build incubators for innovation, upgrade traditional industries, develop emerging industries, and deploy future industries," Xi said of his proposed BRICS initiatives. Trump and Xi are scheduled to meet on September 24 at the White House. The leaders' comments come as both OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei have called for cooperation between the US and Chinese governments to pace and regulate the development of frontier AI models. Altman said in a Sunday interview with Fortune that Trump and Xi should get the Nobel Peace Prize if they can agree on shared rules on the safe development of AI. "Even if just the US and China could agree on some shared standards and testing for development of this technology, I think that'd be a wonderful accomplishment that the two of them can deliver," Altman said. He didn't specify what those standards would look like, but said it wouldn't be hard to create, calling it akin to a "one-page document." Amodei, in an interview with CBS released on Sunday, said the US should talk with the Chinese and work together to "put a speed limit on the rate of this technology." The debate about whether AI has the capacity to bring about the apocalypse has reached a fever pitch. Last week, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit the company, saying neither OpenAI nor Anthropic was acting responsibly and they were "gambling with our lives." He said the people building this technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." Several OpenAI and Anthropic staff have since followed his lead, posting about what they say is AI's potential to wipe out humanity if it's allowed to develop unchecked. Jump to

The programme is intended to support up to a 2-gigawatt buildout by 2027. The expansion focuses on adding land, power and data centre shell capacity at sites designed to host multiple generations of NVIDIA DSX systems. Participating providers will operate the facilities, while NVIDIA will supply the DSX platform, computing systems, networking, software and ecosystem support. Demand for AI computing has risen as companies, researchers and public sector bodies seek more local access to large-scale infrastructure for training and deploying models. The broader buildout is intended to serve Australian startups, universities, researchers, developers, enterprises and AI-focused companies. NVIDIA also tied the expansion to broader use of its Nemotron open models in Australia, saying greater local access to computing resources and models would help organisations develop regional applications and agents for domestic industries. **Partner buildout** Several participating groups also outlined separate projects under the wider programme. Firmus is extending its Project Southgate initiative, which is intended to support demand from hyperscale operators and AI-focused customers in Australia and the Asia-Pacific region. “Project Southgate represents a tangible commitment to building Australia's AI future,” said Oliver Curtis, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Firmus. “Together with NVIDIA, we are developing AI factories that will give Australian businesses, researchers and innovators access to world-class computing capacity at home, while positioning Australia to meet growing AI demand across Asia-Pacific,” Curtis said. Sharon AI is deploying up to 68,000 NVIDIA GPUs linked with NVIDIA Quantum InfiniBand and NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. The infrastructure is intended to support startups, enterprises and research organisations. “Australia has the energy, connectivity and ambition to lead in AI. That potential only becomes real capability when organizations can access world-class compute without compromising on security or sovereignty,” said James Manning, Co-Founder and CEO of Sharon AI. “By building on NVIDIA's DSX platform, Sharon AI is equipped to bring gigawatt-scale AI factories to Australian enterprises, researchers, government and AI natives. With the trust and reliability needed to build, train and deploy AI at scale, Australia can turn its natural advantages into a genuine national AI capability,” Manning said. Infra & Chips.content: Posted: # AI infrastructure company Cornelis raises $205M to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance Cornelis, a company creating networking technology to help AI chips communicate more effectively, announced Monday that it has raised $205 million in a funding round led by IAG Capital Partners. It also announced a product called Active Compute Fabric, a network technology that targets the fact that much GPU time is wasted waiting for data to arrive. Cornelis hopes to address this with a networking fabric that lets chips process and send information at the same time. The company, which spun off from Intel in 2020, is competing with Nvidia by offering an open architecture, meaning customers can use a variety of GPU and accelerator hardware with Cornelis’ networking fabric. Though Nvidia chips can technically run on other networking fabrics, they’re optimized to run on Nvidia’s own software, making it much easier — and more enticing — for customers to use Nvidia’s full GPU stack. Cornelis is part of a new wave of AI infrastructure companies emerging to break apart Nvidia’s market dominance, piece by piece (or chip by chip, one could say). Cornelis has already started shipping its product and is working on a new generation of it, expected to be released later this year. Last day to book an exhibit table is September 18. Don’t miss out on high-impact leads, investor access, and a brand spotlight in Disrupt’s Expo Hall. ### Newsletters Subscribe for the industry’s biggest tech news

AI-RTZ #1209 ### ...no AI security drama at Nvidia, and a high-growth AI roadmap driven by methodical, annual execution. [Michael Parekh](https://substack.com/@michaelparekh) Nvidia founder/CEO [Jensen Huang](https://michaelparekh.substack.com/p/ai-nvidias-jensen-huang-in-peak-paranoid) continues to differentiate himself vs US peers and customers in this [AI Tech Wave](https://michaelparekh.substack.com/p/ai-building-value-over-time). Up and down the tech stack. And the one at the top of the heap, with a $5 trillion plus market cap thus far. While founder/CEOs Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Demis Hassabis, Bill Gates, and others [fret via essays](https://michaelparekh.substack.com/p/ai-the-ai-existential-risk-essays) and posts over AI risks to come, he executes his roadmap with pragmatic precision. As he has done for over three decades. And his growth plans are just starting, as could be seen by his comments at an industry conference last week. I recounted the essays in yesterday’s [Sunday ‘Bigger Picture](https://michaelparekh.substack.com/p/ai-the-ai-existential-risk-essays)’, after Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX’s xAI and Google DeepMind all agreed on Saturday to pace frontier AI progress, and called for government gating on frontier model development. Today’s AI Ramblings Daily podcast, ARD #162, goes into all of that in detail. Watch for its Substack writeup later today as well. Jensen took the other side of that debate at the same Goldman conference on Thursday. [The cybersecurity alarm](https://www.axios.com/2026/09/10/nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-ai-anthropic), he said, is a way to create demand by creating a problem, and the doom talk is nonsense. I sided with him in [Sunday’s piece](https://michaelparekh.substack.com/p/ai-the-ai-existential-risk-essays). Today is about the other half of his week: the growth. TechCrunch lays out the growth plans in *[“Jensen Huang explains why Nvidia will grow an astounding 70% next year”:](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/10/jensen-huang-explains-why-nvidia-will-grow-an-astounding-70-next-year/)* > *“Jensen Huang told attendees at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology conference on Thursday why his company’s AI domination — and revenues — will continue its record-breaking growth streak through the end of next year.”* He addressed investor reservations head-on, as TechCrunch outlined: > *“There’s been endless hand-wringing over whether Nvidia’s party will end as it faces increasing competition for GPUs and AI chips from all directions: the hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, each building their own) and the AI labs (Anthropic and OpenAI, which are building their own), as well as from [newly public competitor Cerebras](https://techcrunch.com/2026/05/17/for-eclipse-the-2-5b-cerebras-win-is-just-the-start-of-realizing-its-physical-world-thesis/) and startups such as [Etched](https://techcrunch.com/2026/06/30/nvidia-competitor-etched-hits-5b-valuation-1b-in-sales-for-ai-chip/).”* And he proceeded to reframe his company’s mission, and its historical transition over the last four years or so in particular: > *“Most people think Nvidia builds a chip. I mean, you need airplanes to ship what we build,” Huang said, adding that the company continues to battle a perception from its early days. Nvidia invented the GPU, which back then were largely sold to consumers to improve PC gaming.”* > > *“One GPU now is not $399. It’s $8.5 million dollars. That’s one GPU, all connected with NVLink, 2 million parts, right? … That’s a GPU, and we ship thousands of them.”* > > *“He added that orders for just one product, [a computer system](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/gb200-nvl72/) that combines 36 Grace CPUs with 72 Blackwell GPUs, is currently experiencing 27% month-to-month sales growth.”* The [whole piece](htt...

Infra & Chips.content: [Skip to content](#main) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) [![Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/ti-eye-logo.webp)](https://tech-insider.org/) [Tech Insider](https://tech-insider.org/) # Fujitsu MONAKA CPU Cuts AI Servers 50% [2026] * [![Elias Virtanen](https://tech-insider.org/wp-content/plugins/one-user-avatar/assets/images/wpua-64x64.png)](https://tech-insider.org/author/elias-virtanen/)[Elias Virtanen](https://tech-insider.org/author/elias-virtanen/ "Posts by Elias Virtanen") * [Hardware](https://tech-insider.org/category/hardware/) [Elias Virtanen](https://tech-insider.org/author/elias-virtanen/) September 15, 2026 12 min read Fujitsu announced on September 14, 2026, from Kawasaki, Japan, that it will begin global sales of FUJITSU-MONAKA, a next-generation CPU designed and built entirely in Japan, starting in November 2026. Alongside the chip, the company is launching the Fujitsu MONAKA Server, a made-in-Japan system the company is positioning as sovereign AI infrastructure for data center operators, enterprises, academic and HPC researchers, and defense agencies in Japan and Europe. The announcement, carried by [PR Newswire](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/fujitsu-launches-made-in-japan-next-generation-cpu-fujitsu-monaka-and-fujitsu-monaka-server-for-sovereign-ai-infrastructure-302877394.html) and confirmed by outlets including [Unite.AI](https://www.unite.ai/fujitsu-unveils-2nm-fujitsu-monaka-cpu-and-sovereign-ai-server/) and [CybersecAsia](https://cybersecasia.net/pr-newswire/fujitsu-launches-made-in-japan-next-generation-cpu-fujitsu-monaka-and-fujitsu-monaka-server-for-sovereign-ai-infrastructure/), marks Fujitsu’s clearest attempt yet to sell Japan and Europe on domestically built AI hardware instead of relying on Nvidia-centric supply chains. The pitch is specific and numerical: Fujitsu says FUJITSU-MONAKA delivers twice the AI inference throughput of comparable CPUs while consuming half the power for the same workload, which the company frames as letting customers run equivalent jobs on 50% fewer physical servers. That claim, paired with a 144-core Arm chip built on a 2nm compute die, puts Fujitsu in direct competition with Nvidia’s Grace CPU, AWS’s Graviton line, and Ampere Computing’s AmpereOne, but with a distinctly different sales pitch built around national security and supply-chain traceability rather than raw benchmark supremacy. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. [Add Now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Ftech-insider.org%2F) ## What Is FUJITSU-MONAKA? Inside the 2nm, 144-Core Arm Chip FUJITSU-MONAKA is a 144-core Armv9-based server processor built from four 36-core compute chiplets. According to technical breakdowns published by [Tom’s Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/cpus/fujitsu-flaunts-144-core-monaka-cpu-2nm-and-5nm-chiplets-soic-and-cowos-packaging) and [ServeTheHome](https://www.servethehome.com/fujitsus-arm-based-monaka-data-center-cpu-at-hot-chips-2026/), the compute chiplets are fabricated on TSMC’s N2 (2nm) process and stacked face-to-face onto SRAM cache tiles built on TSMC’s N5 (5nm) process, joined with hybrid copper bonding rather than a conventional interposer. Fujitsu first demonstrated this 3D-stacked packaging approach at the Hot Chips 2026 conference, months before confirming a commercial launch date, which is why the deepest architectural details trace back to that earlier technical disclosure rather than the September 14 sales announcement. The commercially available FUJITSU-MONAKA CPU tops out at a 3.8GHz clock speed with a memory transfer rate of 8,800MT/s, and it includes dedicated matrix-multiplication instructions alongside Arm’s SVE2 vector extensions...
